title: Narada, the boy who listened
hookLine: a servant's son overhears the sages singing
carry: satsang: love for God is caught in company
tomorrow: a hunter who left animals half-dead ends up sweeping ants off his path. how?

cards: In the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Vyasa has finished the Mahabharata, and he feels strangely empty. The sage Narada visits and tells him a story about himself.
In an earlier life, Narada says, I was the son of a maidservant. One year, a group of sages stayed near us through the rainy season, and I was set to serve them, just a small boy.
I fetched things, kept quiet, didn't play. Once, with their permission, I ate what was left on their plates. And every day I heard them sing and talk about Krishna.
Nobody gave me a lesson. I just listened. And somewhere in those months a taste for those stories woke up in me, and it never left.

teach.h: THE IMAGE, THE BOOK, THE COMPANY.
teach.b: Rupa's list of devotional practices runs long: honoring a teacher, keeping fast days, waving lamps before the image, and far more. Then he circles a handful with a strange and wonderful power.

In paraphrase: serving the sacred image with love and faith. Tasting the meaning of the Bhagavata with people who relish it. The company of devotees who are like-minded, affectionate and further along.
Singing the name. And living in the land of Mathura, where Krishna's stories happen. Now look at the boy.
He had three of those without trying: the company, the stories, the singing. Then Rupa's promise. Let faith be far off, he says.
Even a slight connection with these can give birth to bhava, the deeper love, in a clear-minded person. A child doing chores at the back of the room is that slight connection.

teach.h: SATSANG: LOVE IS CAUGHT IN COMPANY.
teach.b: Hindus call this satsang, the company of the true. As many teachers put it, love for God is caught from people who already have it more than it's taught.

It's one reason temples hold kirtan, and families bring sleepy kids to the Sunday program. On Mathura, readers differ: some take it as living there in body, others as dwelling there in mind, through its stories.

how: In Gaudiya Vaishnava communities, devotees gather to sing Krishna's names, hear the Bhagavata together and serve the temple image, and some make pilgrimage to the Mathura region.

games.q: Narada was a small servant boy, with no lessons and hardly any faith yet. by Rupa's promise, what could a few months near the singing sages do?
o: even a slight connection can give birth to the deeper love.
nothing, until a teacher certifies their faith as strong.
steady their mood for a day, and then fade.
games.why: Let faith be far off, Rupa says: a little contact with these practices can give birth to bhava in a clear-minded person.

practice: Hum the first line of a bhajan or kirtan you know, or, if none comes, one long, low note, and feel where it buzzes: the lips, the throat, the middle of the chest.
Then hum it again, and hold in mind the voices you've sung with, at a temple, a birthday, as if they were singing too. If you pray, let the line carry Krishna's name; if not, let it carry the people.

wordCard.voice: Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu: a book that circles a few practices, mostly shared ones, and promises that even a slight touch of them can wake the deeper love.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi Mathura, the land of Krishna's stories; living there is one of the practices Rupa circles.

carryVoice: Your line: satsang. Love for God is caught in company, the way a servant's boy caught it. One more day in Rupa's ocean.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 1.5.23–26 (Narada tells Vyasa of his former birth as a maidservant's son serving sages through the rainy season; with their permission he ate their remnants; hearing them, a taste for Krishna's stories arose)

Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.2 (eastern division, second wave): the most potent limbs of practice: serving the image with faith, relishing the Bhagavata with those who savor it, company of like-minded affectionate devotees, singing the name, living in the Mathura region
Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.2 (following verse): let faith be far off; even slight connection with these gives birth to bhava in the clear-minded
